name: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour
aliases: phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour, mixed connective tissue variant

clinicalPearls: A usually benign mesenchymal tumour that secretes fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), causing renal phosphate wasting and the syndrome of tumour-induced (oncogenic) osteomalacia
Patients present with chronic bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue and fragility fractures, often after years of misattributed symptoms
Biochemistry shows hypophosphataemia with inappropriately normal or low active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) and raised or inappropriately normal FGF23
Tumours are typically small, slow-growing and occult, arising in bone or soft tissue anywhere in the body, including the extremities, head and neck and acral sites
Histology of the classic mixed connective tissue variant shows bland spindle cells, a distinctive grungy calcified matrix, haemangiopericytoma-like vessels and osteoclast-like giant cells
Recurrent FN1-FGFR1 or FN1-FGF1 fusions are characteristic and reinforce the central role of FGF signalling
Complete surgical resection of the tumour is curative and typically normalises phosphate and reverses osteomalacia
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour causes disease chiefly through overproduction of fibroblast growth factor 23, a hormone that reduces renal reabsorption of phosphate and suppresses activation of vitamin D. The resulting chronic hypophosphataemia impairs bone mineralisation, producing osteomalacia with bone pain, weakness and fractures. Recurrent gene fusions involving fibronectin and FGF receptor or ligand genes are thought to establish an autocrine loop that both drives tumour growth and sustains FGF23 secretion, so that removing the tumour usually corrects the metabolic derangement.
additionalDifferentials: X-linked and autosomal hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets or osteomalacia
Other causes of acquired hypophosphataemia, including drug-induced phosphate wasting
Osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency or malabsorption
Giant cell tumour of bone or soft tissue
Sinonasal haemangiopericytoma (glomangiopericytoma) when in the head and neck
Chondromyxoid fibroma or other matrix-producing tumours
additionalInvestigations: Serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and renal phosphate handling (tubular reabsorption of phosphate)
Serum FGF23 measurement and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level
Functional imaging such as somatostatin-receptor (for example gallium-68 DOTA) PET to localise a small occult tumour
Cross-sectional imaging (MRI or CT) directed to sites highlighted by functional studies
Molecular testing for FN1-FGFR1 or FN1-FGF1 fusions where diagnostically useful
Selective venous sampling for FGF23 when a tumour cannot be localised by imaging
redFlags: Unexplained hypophosphataemia with fragility fractures and progressive weakness
Long-standing bone pain misdiagnosed as another rheumatological or musculoskeletal disorder
Persisting or recurrent hypophosphataemia after apparent resection, suggesting residual or metastatic tumour
Histological features of malignancy in the rare malignant variant
reference.prognosis: The great majority of phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours are benign, and complete tumour resection is curative with rapid normalisation of phosphate and healing of osteomalacia; incompletely excised tumours cause persistent disease, rare malignant examples can recur or metastasise, and when the tumour cannot be located FGF23-directed medical therapy is used to control the metabolic bone disease.
pitfalls: Failing to measure serum phosphate in a patient with chronic bone pain and weakness, so the diagnosis is missed for years
Attributing osteomalacia to vitamin D deficiency without recognising renal phosphate wasting
Not pursuing functional localisation for a small, clinically occult tumour
Overlooking the diagnosis when the tumour is at an unusual acral or head and neck site
Assuming benign behaviour and omitting follow-up biochemistry to confirm cure
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Complete surgical excision with clear margins is the definitive, usually curative treatment, rapidly normalising FGF23 and phosphate
Localise the occult tumour with somatostatin-receptor PET imaging to direct resection or ablation
Bridge or treat unresectable disease with oral phosphate supplementation combined with active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol)
Use the anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody burosumab for inoperable or persistently occult tumours
Monitor phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone, watching for nephrocalcinosis and tertiary hyperparathyroidism from supplementation
Undertake surveillance for local recurrence and the rare malignant, metastasising variant, adding radiotherapy or systemic therapy where malignant
Coordinate management across endocrinology, surgery and specialist pathology
